overview: A string of Pacific systems keeps the Coast Mountains and Cascades wet this week, with snow limited to higher elevations. The northern Rockies stay mostly dry until a stronger system and gusty westerly winds arrive Thursday into Friday.

regions.title: Coast Mountains
regions.text: Rain is the main story here, with snow confined to the high ground. Whistler's 32 inches is the total for the week, and most of it falls Tuesday and Wednesday. Expect mixed precipitation, and rain by Thursday that will turn the upper snowpack heavy and wet.

regions.title: Cascades
regions.text: A series of Pacific fronts brings widespread rain, gusty southeast winds and snow at the higher passes. Mt. Baker leads with 19 inches for the week, Wednesday's 8 inches its biggest day. The National Weather Service is calling for more, 13 to 28 inches at Crystal Mountain from Monday through Thursday night.

regions.title: Northern Rockies
regions.text: Monday brings a passing trough and a chance of light snow across western Wyoming. Tuesday and Wednesday turn drier and milder under a ridge, with breezy winds. Jackson Hole's 9 inches come mostly Thursday and Friday as a stronger system arrives, and the National Weather Service expects more at Grand Targhee, 4 to 12 inches.

regions.title: Kootenays
regions.text: Rain and flurries dominate, with snow mixing in only on Thursday when temperatures sit around freezing. Whitewater and Revelstoke each show 7 inches for the week, with Thursday the best day at both. Expect wet conditions and changing snow levels through the weekend.

ahead.text: The Weather Prediction Center expects a wet pattern to persist through the holiday weekend for the West Coast, with the next system reaching it around Saturday Nov 28 and possibly a deeper trough by Sunday Nov 29.

sources.name: NOAA buoys 51001 / 51101 (method: Powder Buoy, Mike Ruzek)

buoy.text: Buoys 51001 and 51101 near Hawaii popped Nov 11, the swell signal Powder Buoy watches for a Wasatch storm about two weeks later — here Nov 22–28. In past winters a pop raised the chance of a Wasatch storm in that window by roughly 6 to 12 points. Experimental: promising, not proven.
